stem:
$P$, $Q$ and $R$ are points on a circle, centre $O$.
Angle $POR = 116^\circ$.

Find angle $PQR$.
Give a reason for each step of your working.
figure_description: A circle with its centre marked by a small dot labelled $O$. Three points on the circumference, labelled outside the circle in plain capitals: $P$ on the left of the circle a little above the horizontal through $O$, $R$ on the right of the circle a little above the horizontal through $O$, placed so that the angle $POR$ measured through the top of the circle is $116^\circ$ (i.e. $P$ at about $148^\circ$ and $R$ at about $32^\circ$ measured anticlockwise from the rightward horizontal at $O$); and $Q$ at the very top of the circle, on the MINOR arc $PR$, between $P$ and $R$. Draw the two radii $OP$ and $OR$ as solid lines and the two chords $PQ$ and $QR$ as solid lines. Mark the angle $POR$ at $O$ (the angle between the radii, opening upwards towards $Q$) with a small arc and print "$116^\circ$" inside it. Print nothing else: angle $PQR$ is NOT marked, no other angle values, no fourth point, no dashed lines, no shading. The drawing need not be to scale but the $116^\circ$ angle should look obtuse and $Q$ must clearly sit on the shorter arc between $P$ and $R$.
solution:
Reflex angle $POR = 360^\circ - 116^\circ = 244^\circ$ (angles at a point).

Angle $PQR = \frac{1}{2} \times 244^\circ = 122^\circ$ (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; $Q$ is on the minor arc $PR$, so angle $PQR$ stands on the major arc $PR$, which subtends the reflex angle at $O$).

Alternatively: take any point $S$ on the major arc $PR$. Angle $PSR = \frac{1}{2} \times 116^\circ = 58^\circ$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference), and angle $PQR = 180^\circ - 58^\circ = 122^\circ$ (opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$ are supplementary).

Angle $PQR = 122^\circ$.
syllabus_check: 4052 Geometry, properties of circles: angles at a point (the reflex angle at the centre) and the angle at the centre equals twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; the cyclic-quadrilateral route is an accepted alternative. A two-step chain with a reason at each step, 2 marks. No tangent, alternate-segment or other out-of-syllabus result is used.
originality_note: No tangent, no diameter and no external point — every exemplar builds on a tangent or a straight line through the centre. This question uses only the reflex angle at the centre with the angle-at-the-centre property, the diagram (not the stem) placing $Q$ on the minor arc so that the wanted angle is the obtuse one, $122^\circ$. The letters, the $116^\circ$ value and the chain are new.
